Modern.brandNameRationale: Single word. MILL is where the flour begins, and where the bread really starts. Modern in its plainness. The brand puts the source of the bread first, before anyone says the word artisan.
Modern.industrySummary: Sourdough went mainstream during the pandemic. Now every neighborhood has a bakery that calls itself craft. The market is asking for the next step. Something that respects the bread but doesn't worship it.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Tartine (tartinebakery.com) is the canon. Sullivan Street Bakery (sullivanstreetbakery.com) sells the volume. She Wolf Bakery (shewolfbakery.com) does the Brooklyn version. Most lean rustic. We lean modern.
Modern.positioningStatement: A bakery for people who care about the bread and don't need the wood-and-flour story.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 50. Eats out three nights a week. Cooks the other four. Knows which bakery a chef uses. Will drive across town for a good loaf. Doesn't need the loaf wrapped in butcher paper to know it's good.

dos: Use bread terms accurately
List what's in the loaf
Update the menu like a software changelog

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. MILL set in a precise grotesk, wide kerned, all caps. A small secondary mark, a single grain of wheat reduced to its silhouette, used as the app icon and on the take-home box stamp.

Modern.tagline: A working bakery, six loaves a day.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Loaf is the plain trade noun; Atelier is the French studio-and-workshop suffix that's been borrowed by modern bakeries to signal craft (Lune Croissanterie, Apollonia Bakehouse, Hart Bageri). Together the name reads as a small working bakery with a craftshop register, in the lineage of Tartine, Sullivan St, and Hart Bageri — a step elevated from 'Bakery' without going aspirational.
Modern.manifesto: Most neighbourhood bakeries try to be everything at once — twelve breads, fifteen pastries, sandwiches, coffee, cakes for order. We started Loaf Atelier because a working bakery is more honest as a small daily list. Six loaves, four pastries, one cake. Baked through the night. Sold from the counter from seven. When they're gone the door says SOLD OUT.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern neighbourhood bakeries have matured into a category dominated by the Tartine model (broad menu, broad day) and the croissanterie model (single product, deep). The opening is for a small daily-quantity bakery — fewer items, baked once, sold until gone, no afternoon restock.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Tartine (tartinebakery.com) is the broad-menu reference. Hart Bageri (hartbageri.com) plays in the small-list Copenhagen peer slot. Sullivan St Bakery (sullivanstreetbakery.com) holds the New York peer position. Lune Croissanterie (lunecroissanterie.com) is the single-product reference. We sit alongside Hart Bageri with a daily-quantity model.
Modern.positioningStatement: Loaf Atelier is a small working bakery selling a fixed daily list — six loaves, four pastries, one cake — and closing when it's gone.
Modern.positioningRationale: We compete on daily discipline. The list does not grow. The shop sells until the list runs out, and then the door closes. Morning queue is the marketing.

Luxury.tagline: Bread, since attention was a virtue.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: An English baker's name passed down a generation, with a deliberate twist. Daughters, not Sons. It says heritage without nostalgia. The name sounds like a small institution that already exists. People assume it has been here longer than it has.
Luxury.story: Hawkins & Daughters began with a single oven in a stone room and a family that kept showing up to it. We grew slowly, by intention. We still make the same number of loaves a day as the day we opened. Some people wait. Most do.
Luxury.industrySummary: There's a luxury food market that has run out of objects to elevate. Chocolate, salt, olive oil, even ice cubes. Bread sits there still. Plain on the counter. We think that's the opportunity.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Poilâne (poilane.com) wrote the playbook. Du Pain et des Idées (dupainetdesidees.com) holds the Parisian charm. Tartine (tartinebakery.com) goes American luxury. We are quieter than all of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: The bread house for people who treat bread the way other people treat wine.

targetAudience.primary: 40 to 70. Wealthy. Has a chef at home or knows the chef at the restaurant. Eats bread the way it was meant to be eaten, with salted butter and silence. Will pay twelve dollars for the right loaf.

dos: Speak slowly
Use accurate French where it fits
Name the flour, the mill, and the miller

Luxury.tagline: A Paris bakery. Two breads. Three pastries.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: Boulangerie is the French word for bakery — instantly placing the brand in the Parisian artisan tradition. Vérin is a plausible French surname (the founders' family name) following the convention of single-surname boulangeries: Poilâne, Du Pain et des Idées, Maison Kayser. The 'Boulangerie [Surname]' format is the gold-standard convention for serious French bakeries — heritage, family-owned, intentionally narrow catalog.
Luxury.story: Boulangerie Vérin is a Paris bakery founded in 1947, now run by the founder's grandchildren. The catalog runs to two breads and three pastries. The shop has been at the same address for seventy-eight years. The current head baker trained under the founder's son for twelve years before taking the lead.
Luxury.industrySummary: Paris artisan bakeries dominate the global premium reference set. There is space for a small, heritage, family-owned boulangerie with a deliberately narrow catalog — closer to Poilâne or Du Pain et des Idées than to Maison Kayser's multi-city operation.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Poilâne (poilane.com) is the family-heritage reference. Du Pain et des Idées (dupainetdesidees.com) holds the small-catalog peer slot. Maison Kayser (maison-kayser.com) sits in the multi-shop heritage peer. Tartine (tartinebakery.com) is the American premium reference. We belong with Poilâne and Du Pain et des Idées with a more narrowly held catalog.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A 1947 Paris boulangerie in third-generation family operation, with two breads and three pastries, baked the same way since the founder.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We do not extend the catalog. The bakery is the limit. The two breads and three pastries have remained the same across three generations, with continuity of recipe, of staff, and of address.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. Crumb is what bakers obsess over: the inside of the loaf, the air pockets, the texture. The brand is named after the part of the bread that only the baker thinks about. Quietly opinionated.
Minimal.industrySummary: There are too many bakery brands. Every one of them has a story, a logo, a sourdough origin tale. Most of them are good. Almost none of them are quiet.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Tartine, Du Pain et des Idées, every neighborhood Brooklyn bakery. The reference shelf is full. The shelf for quiet is empty.
Minimal.positioningStatement: The bakery that doesn't make a fuss about being a bakery.

dos: Say less

customSections.body: No bag art. No founder story. No social campaigns. No paper price tags written by hand. Plain printing, plain paper.

Minimal.tagline: One word. One bakery. One bread a day.
Minimal.brandNameRationale: Crumb is the baker's trade term for the inside of a loaf — the texture, the open structure, the air. It's a real bakery-vocabulary word, single-syllable, archaic in everyday English. Reads as honest, slightly nerdy in the way bakers are nerdy. Stands in the lineage of single-word trade-specific bakery names — closer to Tartine's botanical naming than to anything literal.
Minimal.manifesto: Bakeries advertise variety. Eighteen breads, twenty-five pastries, sandwiches, soups, cakes for order. We made Crumb because the only thing the shop sells is the daily bread — one variety, baked overnight, sold from the counter until it's gone. The shop is one room. The menu is one line. The customer comes for the bread.
Minimal.industrySummary: Single-product bakeries (the croissanterie, the sourdough-only) have proved that minimal catalogs work in the premium bread category. There is real space for a single-bread bakery that takes the minimal premise even further — one bread, one counter, one page on the site.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Lune Croissanterie (lunecroissanterie.com) holds the single-product reference. Hart Bageri (hartbageri.com) plays in the small-catalog Copenhagen middle. Bread Ahead (breadahead.com) sits in the bakery-school peer position. Tartine (tartinebakery.com) is the broader premium reference. We sit further out — one bread, posted daily.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Crumb is a one-bread bakery selling a single overnight-baked loaf, from the counter, until it sells through.
Minimal.positioningRationale: We strip the catalog to one item. The bread is posted daily. The shop closes when the bread runs out.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Atlas signals scale and reliability without trying. Bakehouse is honest about what we do, not dressed up as artisanal. Co. closes it like a real business. The whole thing reads as a vendor a procurement team would already trust.
Corporate.industrySummary: Restaurants and grocers spend more than they should on bread because the supplier is unreliable. The category is dominated by either huge factory bakers or precious craft bakeries that can't scale. Few players sit in the middle.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Aryzta (aryzta.com) is the industrial giant. Boudin (boudinbakery.com) handles the West Coast wholesale. La Brea Bakery (labreabakery.com) is the premium wholesale standard. We are smaller, faster, more direct.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Wholesale bread that arrives at six, every day, and tastes like it was baked in a real oven.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Restaurant operations live and die on delivery reliability. We compete on showing up first, with bread that the head chef approves the first time.

Corporate.tagline: Wholesale and retail bakery, four generations.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Halverson is a Scandinavian surname common across the American upper Midwest and Pacific Northwest, where wholesale baking has a strong heritage. Baking Co. is the long-standing trade-name suffix used by regional commercial bakers — the structure that signals 'we supply your supermarket bread aisle' more than 'we sell single croissants'. The pair places the brand in the regional wholesale baking tradition (Franz Bakery, Dave's Killer Bread before its acquisition, Nature's Own).
Corporate.manifesto: Halverson Baking Co. is a fourth-generation wholesale and retail bakery supplying grocery chains, foodservice operators, and a small number of company-owned retail bakeries. The buyer is a grocery retail buyer, a foodservice procurement officer, or a private-label client. The contract is multi-year. The metric is consistency, lead time, and shelf life.
Corporate.industrySummary: Wholesale bakery is consolidating under a small number of regional operators (Bimbo, Franz, Flowers Foods). The opening is for a serious mid-tier wholesale bakery with strong retail relationships, modern food-safety operations, and the family-owned continuity grocery buyers increasingly value over private-equity-owned competitors.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Franz Bakery (franzbakery.com) is the Pacific Northwest regional peer. Flowers Foods (flowersfoods.com) holds the multi-brand reference. Pepperidge Farm (pepperidgefarm.com) sits in the premium retail-brand middle. Dave's Killer Bread (daveskillerbread.com) is the modern peer at scale. We belong with Franz Bakery in the regional family-owned wholesale category.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Halverson Baking Co. is a fourth-generation regional wholesale bakery supplying grocery, foodservice, and company-owned retail across the upper Midwest.
Corporate.positioningRationale: We compete on production capacity, lead-time reliability, and the multi-generational family ownership grocery buyers prefer when consolidating supplier relationships.

Creative.tagline: Membership has its perks. Also: cookies.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Crust is the most flavorful part. Club implies you belong. The pair sounds like a place that throws a good party. The name lives on a hoodie before it lives on a sign.
Creative.manifesto: We started Crust Club because we wanted a bakery that felt like a place to hang out. Not a museum. Not a temple. Not a TikTok set. A real bakery with a sticky door handle and a sticker wall and bread that ruins other bread for you.
Creative.industrySummary: Bakeries got serious. The serious ones are great but they're not fun. There's room for one that has personality, throws events, sells T-shirts, and still makes really good bread.
Creative.competitorLandscape: She Wolf Bakery (shewolfbakery.com) is Brooklyn earnest. Bub and Grandma's (bubandgrandmas.com) has the LA charm. Levain (levainbakery.com) figured out the line-out-the-door bakery. We're more clubhouse than counter.
Creative.positioningStatement: The bakery that throws the party and makes the bread.

Creative.tagline: Baked with whatever the air gave us.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Wild Yeast names the airborne natural starter that distinguishes serious sourdough from commercial bread. The name reads as bakery-nerdy in a way that the right customer immediately recognizes and the wrong customer just hears as warm — both effects are useful. The 'Wild [trade element] Bakery' format borrows from the wild-fermentation school of craft brewing (Jester King, The Rare Barrel) translated into the bakery context.
Creative.manifesto: Most craft bakeries try to sound mid-century. The wheat sheaf, the typography, the Parisian inflection. We started Wild Yeast because the actual interesting thing in modern baking is fermentation — the starter that lives in a jar in the kitchen, the slow rise, the airborne natural yeast that gives each batch its particular crumb. The bakery is named after the thing that does the work. The brand is honest about being a science project that became a shop.
Creative.industrySummary: Sourdough and wild-fermentation baking have become well-known to bread enthusiasts but most bakeries don't put fermentation at the center of their brand. There is real space for a creative-led bakery that brands itself around the starter — its age, its provenance, its quirks — and treats the customer as someone interested in the science.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Tartine (tartinebakery.com) holds the broad-market reference for sourdough. Acme Bread (acmebread.com) is the long-tradition peer. Apollonia Bakehouse (apolloniabakery.com) plays in the considered-modern middle. The Sourdough School (sourdough.co.uk) sits in the educational-brand position. We belong alongside Tartine with a louder, more fermentation-forward voice.
Creative.positioningStatement: Wild Yeast Bakery is a sourdough-and-wild-fermentation bakery that puts the starter at the centre of the brand.
Creative.positioningRationale: The starter is the brand. Every loaf is labeled with the starter generation, the bulk-ferment time, and the bake number. The site has a page for the starter — when it was first cultivated, what flours it's been fed, where it lives.
